Omarchy is just an opinionated arch setup, not a foundational project like Ladybird; commenter questions why the two were sponsored together.
Downloading the Omarchy 3 ISO last week sat at about 600 KiB/s; sponsorship's bandwidth support appreciated.

Instead of an installer script, Omarchy now ships a 7GB ISO bundled with Zoom, Spotify, Hey, Basecamp, Steam, Minecraft, etc., but still uses Arch's own package mirrors - critic says this 'makes no sense' compared to a lean install script or true derivative distro.
I cannot for the life of me understand the Omarchy hype. The Linux community has been theming their distribution installs for decades. What distinguishes this from that?
The momentum Omarchy has is impressive - even Framework's CEO has submitted pull requests to the project.
Omarchy now has a dedicated security team (omarchy.org/security/) and is being funded with a reported $10M chest to improve security over time.
Critique: Omarchy's implementation is 'lines and lines of bash script' - like washing a car with sandpaper instead of soap and water.
Security bugs cited include video-title bash injection and notifications being able to run arbitrary bash on the machine.

After a horrible experience with highly-praised CachyOS, user finally tried Omarchy: install was uncomplicated, tiling WM worked like they already use on Mac, terminal tools were great, and installing software was easy and lightning-fast.
Many SSH/security complaints about Omarchy stem from Arch's own default settings, which would be identical on vanilla Arch.
Omarchy's plugin ecosystem is a free-for-all like the Arch AUR, but its audience includes Linux newcomers less able to judge the risks.
I want to love Omarchy but replacing the boot splash screen with its logo is rough; I wish there was a clear way to disable that.
The real story with Omarchy is Hyprland - it's the first time desktop Linux feels fun, with nice defaults for a tiling paradigm that doesn't make people want to smash their computer.

Setting the download property on all screenshot image anchors on the Omarchy site clogs up the Downloads folder and even sets content-disposition:attachment on image responses so they can't be viewed inline.

I like Omarchy but ultimately settled on CachyOS + Hyprland with ML4W dotfiles, benefiting from CachyOS kernel optimizations; Omarchy is the only Hyprland spin that keeps Bash as default shell instead of Fish.
Omarchy fixed the frustration of manually setting up Arch+Hyprland three times with popular dotfiles, which was 'terrible, frustrating and things broke all the time.'
Omarchy installs proprietary software and codecs out of the box, unlike distros that ship only open-source software and then break media playback for newcomers who give up and reinstall Windows.
Omarchy ships Chromium instead of Firefox but the manual just says 'Browser' without noting this anywhere.
Con: Omarchy is designed as a single-user setup with full-disk encryption straight to one user, so it's not ideal for a shared PC - you'd need to run the install script separately per user.

Omarchy's install script silently enables the chaotic-aur repo (community-built AUR packages) via 'pacman -U --noconfirm', which the user flags as a real supply-chain attack vector, though not much worse than npm/node.
